analysis.one_liner: Gradually raises the federal minimum wage to $25 an hour and ends all subminimum wages.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with 32 Democratic cosponsors and no Republicans, has been referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee and has received no further action.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would raise the federal minimum wage on a fixed schedule: large corporations (revenue of $1 billion or more, or 500+ employees) would go to $25 an hour by 2031, while smaller employers would get more time, reaching $25 by 2038. The minimum wage would then be automatically adjusted each year to stay at two-thirds of the national median hourly wage, so it rises with the economy. It would also phase out every separate lower wage: the tipped minimum wage, the lower wage for newly hired workers under 20, the subminimum wage allowed for workers with disabilities, and the current exemption that lets prisons pay incarcerated workers little or nothing.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers paid at or near the federal minimum, including tipped restaurant workers, newly hired teenagers, workers with disabilities who hold special certificates allowing subminimum pay, and incarcerated workers who currently have no federal wage floor. The bill's findings state the goal is reducing reliance on public assistance and raising purchasing power.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Minimum wage, tipped, disabled, and incarcerated workers

how_it_helps.text: Large employers must raise wages from $12 in 2026 to $25 an hour by 2031; smaller employers get until 2038, so big profitable companies lead the transition.
After the phase-in, the minimum wage is automatically reset every year to two-thirds of the national median hourly wage, so it no longer erodes as prices rise.
Tipped workers would keep every tip they receive by law, and the separate tipped minimum wage would be repealed once their cash wage reaches the full minimum.
The subminimum wage program for workers with disabilities would be phased out, with no new certificates issued and a transition assistance program run by the Labor Department.
Incarcerated workers at public and private facilities would count as employees under wage law for the first time, with room, board, and court fees no longer counted as wages.

analysis.who_pays: Large corporations and smaller employers bear the direct cost of higher payroll, concentrated in low-wage sectors like restaurants, retail, and care services. Sheltered workshops that hold special certificates to pay workers with disabilities less than minimum wage would lose that model. Restaurant operators would have to absorb higher cash wages for tipped staff. Operators of prison work programs would have to pay wages they currently do not.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large corporations, restaurants, and employers of low-wage staff

drawbacks.text: The wage floor would roughly triple from today's $7.25 federal minimum, a very large cost shock for low-wage employers; critics commonly warn of job losses, reduced hours, or higher prices, particularly for small restaurants and care providers, though the bill gives smaller employers a longer runway.

Employers of workers with disabilities under special certificates lose the subminimum model entirely; the bill provides only technical assistance and referrals, and disability-service providers have historically argued that some sheltered jobs disappear when subminimum pay ends.

Requiring wages for incarcerated workers could force corrections budgets and private prison operators to absorb new payroll costs, or lead facilities to scale back or eliminate work programs that inmates use to earn money or reduce sentences.

The bill's own schedule starts at $12 an hour on January 1, 2026, before the bill's enactment and before the Senate has even considered it, which the CBO process it invokes would flag as a cost already in effect the moment of passage.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For low-wage workers the gains are direct and large: a guaranteed path to $25 an hour, tips kept in full, and no legal subminimum wage for anyone. The costs are real but fall on specific employers, and the bill tries to manage them by making the biggest corporations move first and giving smaller employers seven extra years. The main honest concern is the pace: a near-tripling of the federal floor in five years for large employers is faster than past increases, and the disability and prison provisions would end long-standing employment arrangements that some workers and providers value. On balance the bill transfers income from employers of low-wage labor to low-wage workers, which is its stated purpose.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee, which has not taken it up; Congress is still in session, so the bill is sitting in committee.

narrative.text: Representative Delia Ramirez introduced the Living Wage For All Act on April 28, 2026.
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Education and Workforce, where it has remained.
Thirty-two Democratic representatives cosponsored the bill; no Republicans are listed.
No markup, committee vote, or floor action appears in the bill's action history.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no outcome has occurred; employers of low-wage labor, including large corporations and restaurant operators, remain unaffected by any federal wage increase because the bill has not advanced.

for.name: Rep. Delia Ramirez
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led its introduction with 24 original cosponsors.

for.name: 32 Democratic cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors, including Reps. Tlaib, Khanna, Jayapal, Casar, Velazquez, and Norcross.

sides.party_line_note: All 33 sponsors and cosponsors are Democrats and none are Republicans, making this a one-party bill at introduction; no opposition votes exist yet because no committee or floor vote has occurred.

industries.note: They would face the steepest schedule, reaching $25 an hour by 2031, under the bill's premise that big profitable firms should lead the transition. Their savings are workers' lost raises.
The bill phases out the tipped minimum wage and guarantees servers keep all tips, so restaurants that currently count customer tips toward staff wages would have to pay much higher cash wages.

The bill bans new special certificates and sunsets the subminimum wage program under Section 14(c), ending their ability to pay disabled workers below minimum wage, with only transition assistance offered.
Private entities running facilities under public contracts would, for the first time, owe wages to incarcerated workers, and room and board could not be counted against pay.

analysis.trajectory: With a Republican-majority Education and Workforce Committee and zero Republican cosponsors, the bill is very unlikely to receive a committee markup or floor vote this Congress. Absent a major shift, it will likely sit without action until the 119th Congress ends in January 2027, the fate of most one-party minimum wage bills.
